title: Centripetal Force
short_intro: Centripetal force is the net inward force directed toward the center of curvature that is necessary for an object to move along a curved path. It is not a fundamental force of nature, but a descriptive role fulfilled by tension, gravity, friction, or the normal force.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Understanding centripetal force formula, uniform circular motion, banking of roads, and conical pendulum kinematics.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Non-uniform circular motion, tangential and radial components of acceleration, rotating reference frames, and fictitious centrifugal force.

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Direction
bullets: Centripetal force always acts orthogonally to the instantaneous velocity vector of the particle.
It points radially inward toward the instantaneous center of the circular path.
It changes the direction of the velocity vector continuously without necessarily changing its magnitude in uniform circular motion.

concept_notes.heading: Origin of Centripetal Force
bullets: Centripetal force is a resultant force, supplied by existing physical interactions such as gravitational force, tension, friction, or electrostatic force.
It does not do any work on the particle in uniform circular motion because the displacement is always perpendicular to the force.
The absence of a sufficient centripetal force results in the particle moving along a path tangential to the circle due to inertia.

concept_notes.heading: Uniform vs Non-Uniform Circular Motion
bullets: In uniform circular motion, the tangential acceleration is zero, and the net force is purely centripetal (radial).
In non-uniform circular motion, both tangential acceleration (due to changing speed) and radial/centripetal acceleration (due to changing direction) coexist.
The total acceleration vector is the vector sum of the radial acceleration and tangential acceleration.

concept_notes.heading: Centrifugal Force in Rotating Frames
bullets: In a non-inertial rotating frame of reference, an outward pseudo force called the centrifugal force appears to act on masses.
The magnitude of the centrifugal force is equal to mω<sup>2</sup>r, directed radially outward from the axis of rotation.
It is introduced to apply Newton's laws of motion within accelerated rotating frames.

derivations.title: Derivation of Centripetal Acceleration and Force
derivations.conditions: Particle moving with uniform speed v along a circular path of radius r.
steps: Consider position vectors r(t) and r(t + dt) subtending a small angle dθ = (v dt)/r.
Express velocity vector as v = v u<sub>t</sub>, where u<sub>t</sub> is the unit tangent vector.
Find the change in velocity vector dv over time dt, noting that the direction of dv points toward the center of the circle.
Take the limit as dt approaches zero to obtain magnitude of acceleration a<sub>c</sub> = v (dθ/dt) = v<sup>2</sup>/r.
Multiply mass m by acceleration a<sub>c</sub> to obtain the centripetal force F<sub>c</sub> = m v<sup>2</sup>/r.

derivations.title: Derivation of Optimum Speed for Banking of Roads
derivations.conditions: Vehicle of mass m moving on a road banked at angle θ with coefficient of static friction μ.
steps: Identify forces acting on the vehicle: normal force N perpendicular to the road, gravitational force mg downward, and frictional force f along the inclined plane.
Resolve forces into horizontal (radial) and vertical components.
Equate vertical components: N cos(θ) = mg + f sin(θ).
Equate horizontal components to the centripetal force: N sin(θ) + f cos(θ) = \frac{m v^2}{r}.
Substitute maximum static friction f = μN to find the maximum safe speed.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Centripetal Force versus Angular Velocity Squared
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin on a Cartesian plot with F_c on the y-axis and ω<sup>2</sup> on the x-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the straight line equals the product of mass and radius (mr), verifying the direct proportionality F_c ∝ ω<sup>2</sup>.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting experimental data plots in objective questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Conical Pendulum Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A schematic showing a mass suspended by a string tracing out a horizontal circle, with resolved components of tension T.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the dynamic equilibrium where the vertical component of tension balances weight, and the horizontal component provides the centripetal force.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Deriving periodic time formulas as a function of string length and angle.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Radial vs Tangential Acceleration in Non-Uniform Circular Motion
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A vector diagram at a point on a curved trajectory showing a radial vector pointing inward and a tangential vector perpendicular to it.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Highlights that centripetal force only changes direction, whereas tangential force changes the kinetic energy and speed of the particle.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Distinguishing force components in complex mechanics problems.

solved_numericals.question: A stone of mass 0.5 kg is tied to the end of a string 1.5 m long and whirled in a horizontal circle at a constant speed of 3 m/s. Calculate the tension in the string.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: m = 0.5 kg, r = 1.5 m, v = 3 m/s.
Apply the centripetal force formula: F_c = m * (v^2) / r.

solved_numericals.question: A particle of mass 0.2 kg moves in a circle of radius 1.0 m with an angular velocity that increases according to ω = 2t rad/s. Find the total force acting on the particle at t = 1 s.
solution_steps: Calculate angular velocity at t = 1 s: ω = 2(1) = 2 rad/s.
Calculate radial acceleration a_c = ω^2 * r = (2^2) * 1.0 = 4 m/s^2.
Calculate tangential acceleration a_t = α * r = 2 * 1.0 = 2 m/s^2.
Determine total acceleration a_net = sqrt(a_c^2 + a_t^2) = sqrt(4^2 + 2^2) = sqrt(16 + 4) = sqrt(20) = 2√5 m/s^2.
Calculate total force F_net = m * a_net = 0.2 * 2√5 = 0.4√5 N.

solved_numericals.question: Find the maximum speed at which a car can safely negotiate a unbanked circular curve of radius 50 m if the coefficient of friction between the tires and the road is 0.6. (Take g = 10 m/s^2)
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: r = 50 m, μ = 0.6, g = 10 m/s^2.
Set maximum friction equal to centripetal force: μmg = m * (v^2) / r.
Cancel mass m from both sides: v^2 = μ * g * r.
Take square root: v = √300 = 10√3 m/s ≈ 17.32 m/s.

assumptions_and_limitations: Centripetal force formulas assume an inertial frame of reference unless a pseudo centrifugal force is explicitly incorporated in rotating frames.
For macroscopic objects, macroscopic friction and normal reactions are treated as continuous rather than discrete molecular interactions.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Centrifugal force is a real outward force exerted by the center on the revolving body.
common_misconceptions.correct: Centrifugal force is a fictitious force experienced only in a non-inertial rotating frame of reference.
common_misconceptions.why: In an inertial frame, only inward centripetal forces act; outward forces do not exist physically on the mass.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Centripetal force does work on an object in uniform circular motion.
common_misconceptions.correct: Centripetal force does zero work on an object in uniform circular motion.
common_misconceptions.why: Work is the dot product of force and displacement. Since the centripetal force is perpendicular to the displacement vector at every instant, the work done is zero.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Centripetal force is a distinct, new type of fundamental force like gravity or electromagnetism.
common_misconceptions.correct: Centripetal force is a functional label given to any net inward force acting on a circular path.
common_misconceptions.why: Gravity, tension, or friction individually or collectively serve as the centripetal force depending on the physical context.

quick_revision: Centripetal force always points radially inward and has a magnitude of m v^2 / r or m ω^2 r.
Centripetal Force (Angular form): F_c = m \omega^2 r
